why_this_matters: Day 163 sits in Phase 9 (Excel + Power BI + Tableau), whose goal is: Be dangerous in the BI stack that most employers actually use. Today's core material - Bar, line, scatter, area, map, treemap, Dual axis and combined charts, Dashboard layout and device preview - is the vocabulary the rest of the phase is built on. Learners who skip the concept and jump to copying code usually stall two weeks later; the goal here is that you can explain what you did, not just that it ran.

concept.how: Work through the topic cards in order: read the linked source moment, run the linked repository code, then answer the reflection prompts in your own words before moving on.
concept.intuition: Treat each topic as a question the instructor was answering. Find the question, then the answer becomes memorable.
concept.analogy: Building this phase is like learning to drive: watching is not enough, and neither is memorising the manual. You need wheel time on real datasets.
concept.internals: Use the linked notebooks to see real implementations, then step one level deeper: for each library call, ask what data structure and loops it replaces.
concept.visual: Sketch the pipeline of today's topic yourself: inputs -> processing -> outputs. The diagram section contains a generated structure you can copy.
concept.deep: Advanced learners: implement the smallest possible version of today's topic from scratch (no library) before using the library version.
concept.math: Identify which quantity in today's topic is being summed, averaged, or maximised. That quantity is the maths to understand first.

code.heading: **Plot the Pie Charts of the Categorical Object Features**
code.code:
geography_counts = df_train['Geography'].value_counts()

# set the color palette other than viridis
custom_palette = sns.color_palette("Set2", n_colors=3)

# create subplots
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))

# plot the pie chart of 'Geography'
axes[0].pie(geography_counts, labels=geography_counts.index, autopct='%1.1f%%',
            startangle=90, wedgeprops={'linewidth': 1, 'edgecolor': 'white'}, colors=custom_palette)
axes[0].set_title('Geography Distribution')
axes[0].axis('equal')

# plot the pie chart of 'Gender'
gender_counts = df_train['Gender'].value_counts()
axes[1].pie(gender_counts, labels=gender_counts.index, autopct='%1.1f%%',
            startangle=90, wedgeprops={'linewidth': 1, 'edgecolor': 'white'}, colors=custom_palette)
axes[1].set_title('Gender Distribution')
axes[1].axis('equal')

# adjust the layout and show the plots
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('figures/categorical_features_piechart.png')
plt.show()

code.heading: Defining a Function to `Analyse` the `churn rate` with differen `Features` of the Data_set.
code.code:
def pie_bar_plot(df, col, churn_col):
    # Set the color palette
    background_color = '#1a1a1a'
    border_color = '#004080'
    text_color = '#d9d9d9'

    # Extract value counts for the specified column
    value_counts = df[col].value_counts().sort_index()

    # Create a DataFrame for the pie chart
    pie_df = pd.DataFrame({'labels': value_counts.index, 'values': value_counts.values})

    # Create a DataFrame for the bar plot
    bar_df = pd.DataFrame({'labels': value_counts.index, 'values': df[df[churn_col] == 1][col].value_counts().sort_index().values})

    # Plotly Pie Chart
    fig = px.pie(pie_df, names='labels', values='values', title=f"Distribution by {col}",
                 labels={'labels': f"Distribution by {col}"},
                 color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2)

    fig.update_traces(textinfo='percent+label', pull=[0.1] * len(pie_df), hoverinfo='label+percent')

    # Update layout for the first subplot (Pie chart)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(font=dict(size=14, color=text_color)),
        paper_bgcolor=background_color,
        font=dict(color=text_color),
    )

    # Plotly Bar Chart
    bar_fig = px.bar(bar_df, x='labels', y='values', title=f"Churn Rate by {col}",
                     labels={'labels': f"Churn Rate by {col}", 'values': 'Churn Rate'},
                     color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2)

    # Update layout for the second subplot (Bar plot)
    bar_fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(font=dict(size=14, color=text_color)),
        paper_bgcolor=background_color,
        font=dict(color=text_color),
        xaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
        yaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
    )

    # Display both charts side by side
    bar_fig.show()
# ... (truncated)

code.code:
def count_percent_plot(df, col, attrition_col):
    # Set the color palette
    background_color = '#1a1a1a'
    border_color = '#004080'
    text_color = '#d9d9d9'

    # Create a DataFrame for the bar plot
    bar_df = pd.DataFrame({'labels': df[col].value_counts().index, 'values': df[col].value_counts().values})

    # Create a DataFrame for the second subplot
    df['attrition_label'] = np.where(df[attrition_col] == 1, 'Yes', 'No')
    value_2 = df[df['attrition_label'] == 'Yes'][col].value_counts().reindex(bar_df['labels'])
    attrition_rate = (value_2 / bar_df['values'] * 100).values

    # Plotly Bar Chart for Employees by col
    fig = px.bar(bar_df, x='labels', y='values', title=f"Employees by {col}",
                 labels={'labels': f"{col}", 'values': 'Count'},
                 color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2)

    # Update layout for the first subplot
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(font=dict(size=14, color=text_color)),
        paper_bgcolor=background_color,
        font=dict(color=text_color),
        xaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
        yaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
    )

    # Plotly Bar Chart for Employee Attrition by col
    attrition_fig = px.bar(x=bar_df['labels'], y=value_2.values, title=f"Employee Attrition by {col}",
                           labels={'x': f"{col}", 'y': 'Count'},
                           color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2)

    # Update layout for the second subplot
    attrition_fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(font=dict(size=14, color=text_color)),
        paper_bgcolor=background_color,
        font=dict(color=text_color),
        xaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
        yaxis=dict(title=dict(font=dict(size=10, color=text_color))),
    )

    # Display both charts side by side
    fig.show()
    attrition_fig.show()
# ... (truncated)

common_mistakes.mistake: Watching the lecture without running the repository notebook.
common_mistakes.why: Recognition is not recall: code that looked obvious fails the moment you type it yourself.
common_mistakes.fix: For every topic today, run the linked notebook cell, then retype it from memory in your own file.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using Bar, line, scatter, area, map, treemap on data whose types or shape you have not printed.
common_mistakes.why: Most failures in this topic are input problems (dtype, shape, missing values) rather than logic errors.
common_mistakes.fix: Print type and shape immediately before the operation; keep that habit for all 275 days.

debugging.symptom: The linked notebook cell raises ModuleNotFoundError or ImportError.
debugging.cause: Wrong kernel/environment selected, or the library is not installed in the active environment.
debugging.fix: Print sys.executable in the notebook and install into that environment (Day 4).

debugging.symptom: Your output differs from the recording even though the code looks identical.
debugging.cause: Library version differences, a changed default argument, or unseeded randomness.
debugging.fix: Pin versions (requirements.txt), set a random seed, and compare dtypes and shapes, not just values (Day 5).
